opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest gap is really in curation and diversity rather than raw scale. With images, the community has spent years building datasets that are carefully filtered and balanced. ImageNet is the classic example, and later efforts showed that curating web-scale image data so it covers concepts more uniformly makes a huge difference for self-supervised learning.

Video hasn't had that same level of attention yet. A lot of the large video datasets we use are either quite narrow, focused on specific action categories, or they're scraped at scale with very little curation. So you end up with heavy redundancy. Many clips look alike, there's a long tail of content that's barely represented, and the distribution is skewed toward things like human-centric activities filmed from a few typical viewpoints.

There's also a temporal dimension that images just don't have. A lot of video is fairly static. The camera's sitting there, not much is happening, and from a learning perspective those frames carry very little signal about dynamics, physics, or how objects interact. If what we actually care about is models that understand how the world evolves over time, we need data that's rich in motion, interactions, and cause and effect, not just more hours of footage.

So I'd say the priorities are better tools for curating video at scale, ways to measure diversity along the temporal axis and not only the visual one, and broader coverage, things like egocentric data, robotics and embodied interaction, and longer-horizon videos where events unfold over minutes rather than seconds. Closing that gap would let video models benefit from scale the way image models have, and I think it's one of the main things holding back progress toward real world models right now.

r001.rationale: The response calls for better video curation and diversity, but does not say video dataset contents should be transparent and well understood like those of curated image datasets.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether learning from video requires more compute than learning from images.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest gap is honestly just scale and diversity, and the two are kind of tied together. If you look at what happened with images, a lot of the progress in self-supervised learning came from the fact that you could just scrape billions of images from the web, and you'd get this incredibly diverse distribution: different objects, different scenes, different viewpoints, different domains. With video, the situation is very different. The datasets that most of the research community actually works with are things like Kinetics or Something-Something, and those are on the order of a few hundred thousand clips, and they're heavily biased toward a particular slice of the world, mostly human actions, often shot in very particular ways.

So the first problem is just raw quantity. A video is way more expensive to store, to decode, to move around, so even if the raw data exists on the web, the engineering cost of actually using it at the scale we use images is much higher. And that means we've been training video models on something like a thousand times less data than image models in terms of unique content, even though each video contains a lot more pixels.

But I'd say the more important issue is the diversity of the content. A lot of video datasets are curated around action recognition, so they're short, trimmed clips centered on a person doing something. That's a very narrow view of the visual world. If you care about learning how the physical world works, how objects move, how things interact, you want video that captures a huge range of everyday situations, egocentric footage, long uncut sequences, static scenes with subtle motion, not just a basketball highlight reel. We found pretty consistently that when you broaden the pretraining distribution, even without adding more labels, the representations get noticeably better at downstream tasks that have nothing to do with the original curation.

The other piece I'd point to is temporal extent. Most clips are a few seconds long, and that fundamentally limits what kind of temporal structure a model can learn. If you want a model to understand that an object you put in a drawer is still there a minute later, or to reason about cause and effect over longer horizons, you need data that actually contains those longer dependencies. Right now we mostly don't have that in a form that's easy to train on.

And then I'd add one more thing, which is evaluation. With images we had this very clean ecosystem of benchmarks that let you measure whether a representation was actually good. In video, a lot of the benchmarks can be solved by looking at a single frame, so they don't really test whether the model learned anything about motion or dynamics. If the benchmark doesn't reward temporal understanding, it's hard to even know if your dataset is giving you what you want. So I think closing the gap is partly about collecting bigger and more diverse video, and partly about building evaluations that actually force models to use the time dimension.

r001.rationale: The response discusses video dataset scale, diversity, curation, and evaluation, but does not call for dataset contents to be transparent and well understood.

r002.rationale: The response says video data is more expensive to store, decode, and move, and does not state that learning from video requires little or no additional compute compared with image learning.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest gap is in the diversity of the data and how we curate it. With images, we’ve gotten pretty good at building large datasets that cover a broad range of visual concepts. With video, simply having more frames doesn’t necessarily give you more information. A lot of those frames are redundant.

What you really want is diversity in how the world evolves: objects moving, people interacting with things, actions having consequences. And you want tasks that actually require understanding that evolution. If you can solve a video benchmark by looking at a single frame, it’s hard to tell whether your model has learned anything about motion or temporal structure.

So I think the opportunity is both better video data and better ways to measure what models learn from it—particularly things that you couldn’t learn from static images alone.

r001.rationale: The response calls for more diverse video data and better benchmarks, but does not say video dataset contents should be transparent and well understood like curated image datasets.

r002.rationale: The response makes no claim about the compute required to learn from video compared with learning from images.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest gap is the diversity and scale of the data. With images, we’ve gotten pretty good at collecting large datasets that cover a wide range of concepts. With video, having a lot of frames doesn’t necessarily mean you have a lot of diversity. Consecutive frames are often very similar, so the amount of new information you get can be relatively small.

What I’d like to see is more video that captures how the world changes—objects interacting, people manipulating things, and the consequences of different actions. That’s where video can give us something that images can’t: an opportunity to learn about dynamics and to predict what happens next. So I think the challenge is both scaling video datasets and making sure that what we’re scaling contains those rich interactions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses video scale, diversity, and rich interactions, but does not call for dataset contents to be transparent or well understood like curated image datasets.

r002.rationale: The response makes no claim about compute requirements for learning from video compared with learning from images.
